newsitem.title: UK: EBRD plans big funding for Bulgaria privatisation.
newsitem.headline: EBRD plans big funding for Bulgaria privatisation.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said on Sunday that it aimed to extend several million dollars' worth of funding to Bulgaria, which is planning a crash programme of privatisation.

Bulgaria's caretaker government, swept to power amid public protests earlier this year, also promised to privatise the country's six top banks within a year in probably the most ambitious such sell-off in post-communist Europe.

The EBRD's plans are the latest move by an international organisation to help Bulgaria, which is deep in economic crisis, since the reformist government agreed terms with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) last month.
The EBRD's top official responsible for Bulgaria, Olivier Descamps, told Reuters the funding would be in the form of loans and equity stakes in a number of industrial projects.
They involved "several hundreds of millions of potential funding by the EBRD".
"The projects would be worth half a billion dollars," Descamps said during the EBRD's annual meeting in London.
He did not give a figure for the size of the EBRD's contribution to the projects but said the funding could be extended over the next 12 to 15 months.

"We're pushing to play a key role," he said. One Bulgarian project would be announced at the EBRD meeting on Monday in what he called "a large privatisation (with) a large foreign investor". He declined to name the project.
But Bulgarian officials have said there was a good chance the EBRD would take part in privatising major chemical and cement plants.

Earlier this year the EBRD said there were projects in the pipeline that could result in the bank, set up in 1991 to help post-communist Europe to build market economies, committing between $100 and $200 million once the government signed an agreement with the IMF.

Bulgaria agreed a $659 million funding package with the IMF on March 17, which has paved the way for other international groupings to extend extra funding. This included about $400 million from the European Union and the Group of 24 richest countries last week.

International groupings and private investors were wary of investing in Bulgaria due to the slow pace of reform under the former Socialist government of ex-communists which led to the economic crisis.
But that government was swept aside by popular protests in February and the present government has committed Bulgaria to rapid privatisation of industry and banking.
Elections are due on April 19 but the reformist Union of Democratic Forces and its allies are tipped to win.
Earlier Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Bozhkov said Bulgaria aimed to restore confidence in its deeply troubled banking system by privatising its leading six institutions by the middle of next year.
Bozhkov said at a presentation at the EBRD meeting that confidence was returning to the Bulgarian economy in general following the IMF agreement.

The economy was expected conservatively to have shrunk 4.8 percent last year but was beginning to recover in the second quarter of this year. The currency was stabilising and inflation falling to an expected 73 percent in the March-December period.
No former East Bloc nation has tried to privatise six leading banks so quickly since the 1989 fall of communism.
But Bozhkov said speed was essential in implementing long-delayed free-market reforms to take advantage of the current strong public support for the reformist government.
"We aim to boost confidence (in the banking system) with the privatisation of two state banks by the end of September 1997," Bozhkov told bankers from East and West at the presentation.

Agreements to sell two further banks would be reached by the end of this year and the remaining two by the end of June next year. The aim was to come from "a state-dominated banking system to a sound private banking system by the end of 1998".
